segments.text: A supplier you trust sends an invoice. Same logo. Same wording. But the bank details are not theirs.

The email is real. It comes from your supplier's own mailbox, so every check your filter runs, passes. In South Africa, digital banking fraud cost two point four one billion rand in twenty twenty-five. And in the Hawarden case, a buyer paid five and a half million rand to a fraudster. The appeal court ruled the loss was theirs: they could have verified the account details.

Forward it to Is It Legit, and the report fills in live. Before any AI sees the mail, our checks pull out text hidden from the reader, written to steer an AI into calling it safe. They flag a reply address that goes somewhere else, and a link that shows one address and goes to another. Then Muse Spark weighs the evidence and writes the verdict, and every reason it gives cites a finding. The first advice never changes: do not pay until you have called the number in your own records.

Businesses register who they really are: their trading names, their verified domains, and their logo, for SAM 3.1 to compare against the mail. They list the suppliers they pay, with bank details checked only as match or no match. And every check lands in the organisation's cases console, searchable by anyone on the team.

It works both ways. Every morning, the monitor watches over five hundred lookalikes of your domain. Here it caught a live fake Fynbos Freight portal, asking customers to sign in and confirm a new bank account. You see it the same day, so you can warn your customers before they pay.

Under the hood, five Meta models work inside a strict safety contract. Untrusted content stays inside delimited blocks. Critical evidence sets a deterministic floor no model can lower, and every claim must cite an Evidence ID. Even voice notes are decoded in-Worker: a three-second Opus note in {fact.benchNoteOurs}, against FFmpeg's {fact.benchNoteFfmpeg}.

We hold our own models to the same standard. Loupe, our fine-tune of Muse Glimmer thirty B, caught {fact.lureRecallOf} on held-out pages, with {fact.falseAlarmsOf} false alarms, in {fact.latency}. It names the lure type right only about sixty-three and a half percent of the time, and we publish every evaluation run, good or bad.
Your filter protects your inbox. We protect you from everyone else's. Is It Legit, at app.isitlegit.co.za.
